title: Restore justice
hookLine: restore our judges as at first
carry: kindness and justice, from the same throne

lines: THE PLACE YOU GO, BROKEN TOO.
cards: A landlord who ignored the law. A boss who promoted the friend. A court case that dragged on for years and ended with the side that had more money.
A referee who never saw the foul. The trouble isn't just that something went wrong. It's that the place you were supposed to go when things go wrong was broken too.
The eleventh blessing of the Amidah is a prayer about exactly that place.

teach.h: RESTORE OUR JUDGES AS AT FIRST.
teach.b: It says: restore our judges as at first, and our counselors as at the beginning. Remove from us sorrow and sighing. Reign over us, You alone, with kindness and compassion, and vindicate us in judgment.
Blessed are You, King who loves righteousness and justice. The first line is lifted almost word for word from Isaiah.
In the old Jewish translation: "And I will restore thy judges as at the first, and thy counsellors as at the beginning."

Isaiah is speaking to a Jerusalem whose leaders, he says, love bribes and ignore the orphan and the widow. The repair he imagines isn't a new system. It's a return to the old one working the way it should.

teach.h: JETHRO: PEOPLE WHO HATE UNJUST GAIN.
teach.b: Some readers hear in as at first the Torah's picture of judges: when Moses is worn out from judging everyone himself, his father-in-law Jethro tells him to find capable people who fear God, love truth and hate unjust gain.
Notice what sits inside a blessing about justice: kindness and compassion. It doesn't set justice and mercy against each other. It asks for both from the same throne.
It ends with two words a psalm also pairs, saying God loves them: tzedakah and mishpat, righteousness and justice.
And during the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, the ending changes to the King of judgment, because tradition holds that this is the season when God judges the world.

how: Hashivah shofteinu is the eleventh blessing of the weekday Amidah; during the Ten Days of Repentance its closing changes from the King who loves righteousness and justice to the King of judgment.

o: a call to punish the wicked without mercy
a prayer for fair judges, with kindness too
a court ruling that settles a family quarrel

games.q: inside the eleventh blessing — tap the pairs.
p: restore thy judges as at the first
find people who hate unjust gain

s: the blessing sets justice against mercy
it asks God to reign with kindness and compassion, and to judge justly.
the blessing's ending changes between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
it becomes the King of judgment for those ten days.
Isaiah imagines a brand-new system of courts
he imagines judges as at the first: the old system working as it should.

games.q: you're Moses. people line up from morning to evening for you to judge every case. what does Jethro tell you to do?
o: keep going; only you can do it.
find capable, honest people who hate unjust gain to judge with you.
games.why: Jethro tells him to share the work with capable people who fear God, love truth and hate unjust gain.

practice: List, silently, the people who make decisions over your life, a judge, a mayor, a principal, a manager, a landlord, a referee, and pick one, picturing them on an ordinary day with a hard decision on their desk.
Hold one wish for them: that they see clearly, that they can't be bought, that they're kind to the person with the least power in the room. If you pray, you can ask it.

wordCard.voice: Restore justice. Hashivah shofteinu. The Amidah's eleventh blessing: return our judges as at first, with kindness and compassion.

orig.note: Hebrew: restore our judges. the opening of the eleventh blessing, from Isaiah 1:26.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness and justice, from the same throne. A week of requests: bring us back, forgive us, see our trouble, heal us, bless the year, freedom comes first, then gathering, and now fair judges. That's day five hundred eighty-eight.
